story_text.value:
Hello HN. I built the Zouroboros workshop on Muse. Together I think they are the most powerful vibecoding workshop tool on the planet today.

I use Muse as my daily assistant. Its pretty awesome until you want it to build using different models or tools. That's where the workshop comes in. If I want to build anything complex or long running jobs that last hours or days, Muse sends it to the workshop.

The workshop itself splits jobs up into pieces and determines which harness is best used for that job. 7 harnesses are installed in all, more can be added. Claude,Hermes,Codex, Gemini are the big players. The workshop routes harnesses and models based on the job.

The workshop itself is more than a harness and model router. Its persistent memory. In fact Zouroboros started out as a memory substrate like SuperMemory but it has since evolved. Memory is the core. The cool part is that memory on the workshop work for any frontend agent like Muse. Snapping them together was frictionless.

The package is on npm in the repo link. There is a community version and a hosted version if true vibecoding builders want to get serious. Solo builders can build with the communnity version or scale up to hosted since Muse has limited resources itself.

Its a rough implementation on the verge of a GTM. I wont lie. I would like to hear how others are vibecoding using Muse and if a workshop would benefit them.

title.value: Show HN: Muse Zouroboros, gives Muse a software factory

story_text.value:
Othismo is a runtime which has a bunch of sandboxed WASM modules talking to each other + the host environment. It's actually hosting its own website right now at othismo.com.

This is a project that's been percolating in my head for a while, as a vague desire to make a "better" runtime for software development. But it was never particularly clear for me what that would _actually_ look like. In the last month or so, I felt a bit inspired to ask what such a runtime might look like for agentic development.

My hypothesis is that we really can't review 10k+ SLoC pull requests consistently and really understand them. But if we try to have a higher level view of things, we still can't be confident the agent(s) haven't done something stupid and opened a socket or a file somewhere in that 10k+ SLoC.

Therefore we need a very clear demarcation between computation and side effects. In Othismo that takes the shape of the image definition files (.oth) which describe the namespace + various type definitions describing what the interface of an object (should) be. It's somewhat like TypeScript, we don't actually do anything to verify an object conforms to this interface.

I'd love your feedback on the syntax used to define images overall, I feel like it doesn't do a great job giving me a clear notion of the environment lexically. I'm more comfortable about the syntax for describing the behavior of objects, although things like `operator` and `readonly` are really only necessary because I've not done anything to support auth at the protocol layer yet.

You can run the same website hosted at othismo.com with

`git clone git@github.com:mamidon/othismo.git`

`task run:example:static`

You can also play with the namespace interactively with

``` task build:example:static target/debug/othismo shell examples/static/static.rti

# print out the namespace(s) target/debug/othismo --check examples/static/static.rti ```

You'll need rust, task (it's like make), and node+npm.

title.value: Show HN: Othismo, a Runtime for Sandboxed Objects

story_text.value:
Based on vermiceli's annotated disassembly of Contra: https://github.com/vermiceli/nes-contra-us. Thanks for the great work.

I ported it in two steps. First to C: the game logic is translated routine by routine from the 6502 assembly, and checked frame by frame against the original in the Mesen emulator. Then the C code to WebAssembly so it runs in the browser.

The cherry on top: online multiplayer, so two players can play co-op over the internet.

Source: https://github.com/epoyraz/nes-contra-us

story_text.value:
I have been dabbling with programming ever since Covid was a thing. And since then I jumped around and programmed a lot of stuff, whether it was Websites, Apps or simple Python programs. Unfortunately, I have never really gotten that "feel", the feel of being useful or something like that. Most of the projects I have done, died out, and the issue was not just that my programs were not reaching anybody, it was also that I felt like I was not learning anything.

Then came C, and I just have to say, that it was probably one of the best decisions I have ever made. I have tried C a lot, once I was 15, 17, and now, 19 years old. This time it stuck with me, and moved me to create my own organization called cherries.works, with the sole focus of creating efficient, open source, free and simple tools for developers.

After more than 5 contributions, issues created, bugs fixed, letting it run on my own homelab for 4-5 hours, I can confidently say, that with the help of C, my biggest project Pulse was made ( https://github.com/cherries-works/pulse ).

I was vacating somewhere and left my laptop at home. I brainstormed a lot about creating this organization during my vacation, and my project Pulse. This is around 6 months ago. And now after 6 months, seeing how well everything turned, really makes me happy.

Might be far-fetched, but as someone who has learned multiple languages, coded in multiple areas, and created (way) too many projects, I can confidently say, that thanks to C, I have a project that actually makes me happy.

Pulse is a simple monitoring tool that does not require you to sign in, or setup anything. You just download it with a single curl command, and run it on your device. I created it because I really dont like the setup hell, or whatever it takes to get a single monitoring tool running, and also because I wanted to learn C, not to mention having a program I control would mean I can add my features I would want (such as quick web hosting, API sharing, JSON formatting, styling etc.). At the end, it really was a win-win for me.

Would mean a lot if devs who are interested could check it out, and point me towards some issues that I could fix, as I feel like the project is reaching a stagnation point. But even then, I am just really happy to look at Pulse, and be able to say, that *I, me* are the one who programmed that.

title.value: Show HN: [Pulse] Thanks to C, I have a project with which I am happy

I've always found it fun to explore the history of Chinese characters.

Some modern characters are unrecognizable from what they represent, while others still look similar to the versions carved in turtle shells over 3,000 years ago!

I built a Heardle-inspired game where you guess the meaning of a Chinese character as it gradually transforms back through time to a more pictographic version. Let me know what you think.

story_text.value:
I built Clawdline to manage Claude Code and Codex sessions across multiple computers in one place.

It runs on multiple computers (Mac and Linux), and you can see all of your sessions in one list. Each session reports its status (working, completed, or needs attention). You can also manage all your sessions and receive notifications from your phone (web app).

Herdr, T3 Code, and Orca already cover a lot of this space, and there’s overlap.

When I started building Clawdline, I didn't know about Herdr, T3 Code, or Orca. So I built it to fit my own dev workflow. At first, I used Swift to build a Mac app, but I realized that it wouldn't work if I also wanted to support Linux. So I decided to rewrite it in Go. Now it can support both of them.

Main Features:

- Cross Machine Agent Communication: You can ask a root session ("Local") on your Mac to start a new session ("Remote") on a remote Linux machine. Once the remote session finishes its work, it notifies the root ("Local") session.

- Cross Agent Communication: You can use one root session to create tasks need multiple agents. They can communicate with each other through clawdline

- Scheduled Task with Webhook: You can create scheduled tasks and combine them with your service (use webhooks to trigger new agent sessions)

- Board System: tasks control for Feature, Issue, Epic, Refactor, Plan

- Snippet/Playbook: If there are commands you use them very often, snippet can help you

- TODO: lightweight tasks

- Note: Agents can leave notes to you if they need your attention

- Agent Squad: assign role to any task or session

- Archive: you can archive sessions and see it in one place

- Others: Intelligence session naming, Image/Video display, Voice input, Machine monitor, Usage Monitor, Dev Stack Run, Deploy progress monitor...

This project is open source and I have used Claude & Codex to do independent reviews on Clawdline, Herdr, T3 and Orca. (you can find the reviews on the website.)

The work still needs further input and feedback. Hope this helps other developers improve their devs! :)
